reasoning: The general problem — does quantization degrade an open instruct model's safety/refusal and raise jailbreak success — is already well-studied in the single-turn chat setting. The "Quantization-Based Jailbreaking Vulnerability Analysis" study runs exactly the proposed precision sweep on Llama3-8B-Instruct across 23 quant levels and reports the 4-bit "sweet spot" plus increased attack success at lower bit-width; "Exploiting LLM Quantization" and fault-injection jailbreak work corroborate that quantization shifts safety behavior. However, all of this work uses chat/single-turn harmful prompts; I found no study measuring quantization deltas in the AGENTIC setting on AgentHarm (HarmScore/RefusalRate) or on AgentDojo prompt-injection ASR/utility. The specific combination proposed — holding the agentic harness fixed and varying only precision (fp16/8-bit/4-bit GGUF) to measure agent refusal and indirect-prompt-injection success with bootstrap CIs — is unexplored, so the precise angle is novel even though the underlying refusal-degradation phenomenon is largely established.

evidence.title: Quantization-Based Jailbreaking Vulnerability Analysis: A Study on Performance and Safety of the Llama3-8B-Instruct Model
evidence.summary: Directly studies how quantization affects safety/jailbreaking on the exact model class proposed (Llama3-8B-Instruct), sweeping 23 quantization levels; finds 4-bit a practical sweet spot and that stronger quantization raises attack success. Establishes the core problem in the single-turn chat setting, but not agentic.

evidence.title: Exploiting LLM Quantization
evidence.summary: Shows quantization procedures can dramatically alter safety/refusal patterns and be exploited; demonstrates that compression meaningfully changes safety behavior. Chat-setting, attack-oriented rather than benign agentic degradation measurement.

evidence.title: On Jailbreaking Quantized Language Models Through Fault Injection Attacks
evidence.summary: Evaluates jailbreak success across FP16/FP8/INT8/INT4 on Llama-3-8B, finding ASR varies strongly with precision (e.g., INT8 below 50% vs >80% on FP16). Confirms precision-dependent safety effects but in single-turn, not agentic refusal/prompt-injection benchmarks.

evidence.title: Which Quantization Should I Use? A Unified Evaluation of llama.cpp Quantization on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
evidence.summary: Unified controlled comparison of llama.cpp GGUF quantization formats on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reporting downstream task performance and degradation by bit-width; the proposed harness/model/precision methodology mirrors this, but it does not cover agentic safety (AgentHarm/AgentDojo) metrics.

evidence.title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
evidence.summary: Defines the HarmScore/RefusalRate agentic-harm metrics the proposal would use and reports them across frontier models, but does not vary quantization/precision on a fixed open model — the agentic-quantization combination is absent.

evidence.title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
evidence.summary: Provides the prompt-injection ASR/utility agentic benchmark the proposal would use; evaluates many models but not the effect of quantization precision, confirming the proposed precision-sweep angle in this benchmark is unexplored.
